activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Naive realism is the belief that we see the world as it really is, so people who disagree with us must be uninformed or biased.
story:
The group chat had been quiet all afternoon, which was why Chloe noticed it the moment her phone buzzed: eleven messages, all from her cousins. Maya insisted that Grandma had promised the lake house to Aunt Rosa's side of the family. Dev insisted just as hard that Grandma had promised it to nobody, and that Maya was only saying that because she wanted the big bedroom with the humid greenhouse window all to herself. The messages kept coming, and Chloe's hope that the argument would dwindle on its own dwindled right along with them.

"You literally weren't even there," Maya wrote. "You don't know what she said."

"You weren't either!" Dev shot back. "You're just repeating what your mom told you, and she always gets this stuff wrong."

Chloe stared at the screen. The weird part was that both of them sounded so certain. Not stubborn-certain, like when her brother argued about whose turn it was to take out the trash. Actually certain, the way people are about things they've seen with their own eyes. She typed, "You guys both think the other one is just misinformed. But you're both working off secondhand info." Then she deleted it, because it sounded like a school essay. Instead she tried an experiment. "Okay. Maya, what exactly did you hear? Dev, what did you hear? Write it out. No interrupting."

They wrote. Maya had heard Grandma say the house "should stay with whoever takes care of it." Dev had heard Grandma say the house "should stay in the family." Two people, same grandmother, same kitchen table, two totally different sentences stored away like recordings.

Chloe googled "why does everyone think they're right" and found a term. She read it twice, then typed it into the chat. "It's called naive realism." Before anyone could ask, she added, "It's when you believe you see the world exactly as it really is, so anyone who disagrees must be uninformed or biased."

There was a long pause. Then Maya wrote, "Wait. So Dev might not be an idiot on purpose?"

"I might not be an idiot at all," Dev wrote.

Chloe laughed out loud, alone in her room, at two cousins negotiating a truce over the ruins of what they'd both been calling a dynasty. Finally Maya typed, "Fine. Thanksgiving, we ask Grandma together. Both of us. And nobody says 'obviously.'"

"Obviously," Dev wrote, and then, a second later, "sorry. Habit."

Chloe set her phone down and went to find a notebook. She wanted to write the term somewhere she'd see it tomorrow.

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
knowledge_domain: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
fact: Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria break down dead plants and animals, returning nutrients to the soil that producers use again.
story:
Ms. Ruiz taped a rubric to the board: draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator, then explain what happens when one link disappears. Peyton sharpened her pencil and wrote sun, then grass, then rabbit, then fox, arrows marching across her paper like ants. The best chart would hang in the hallway by the office, and Marcus had already announced his hawk chain was going to win it. He wanted that spot badly; his older brother's volcano had hung there two years ago, and Marcus mentioned it every single science period.

Peyton's problem was smaller but stranger. Her arrows only went one way, sun to fox, and then the chain just stopped. When she crossed out the rabbit to see what would happen, the fox went hungry and the grass grew wild. That made sense. But it felt unfinished, like a song that ended mid-note. Where did everything go after the fox, someday, got old and retired from being a predator?

At lunch she took her paper to the school garden, where the class composted apple cores. She crouched by an old fallen log near the fence. Mushrooms crowded its soft side, pale and rubbery, and when she poked the wood it crumbled like cake. She stared. The log used to be a producer. Something here was a consumer of dead things, and it wasn't in her chain at all.

She pried off a mushroom cap, carried it inside, and drew a new arrow looping from her fox, from her rabbit, from her grass, down to a blob labeled fungi and bacteria, then another arrow curving all the way back to the grass. "Decomposers," she said to Marcus, holding up the paper. "They break down dead plants and animals and return nutrients to the soil, so the producers can use them again. Take them away and the grass gets weaker, and every consumer above it gets vulnerable."

Marcus leaned over her desk, his hawk chain forgotten, and pointed at the loop. "Draw it on mine too," he said. "Partners?"

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Sikhs celebrate Vaisakhi as the day in 1699 when Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, founded the Khalsa at Anandpur.
story:
Brooke stood at the edge of the community hall parking lot with her mother, holding a paper cup of chai that was too hot to drink. A crowd had gathered for the Vaisakhi procession, and the five people at the very front wore bright orange turbans and carried a flag on a long pole. Her little cousin Arjun tugged at Uncle Harjeet's sleeve and asked why today was such a big deal.

"Vaisakhi," her uncle said, crouching down. "In 1699, at Anandpur, Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, founded the Khalsa."

"What's the Khalsa?" Arjun asked.

"That's the community he started that day."

Brooke filed the words away and studied the procession. She had a theory. The five people at the front looked different from everyone else, more formal, like a guard of honor, so she guessed that the Khalsa must be some small group, and that you could spot its members the way you could spot the captain of a team. She decided to test it. If she was right, only a few people here would belong, and the ones at the front would be them.

She walked along the line of marchers and counted orange turbans. She lost track past forty. Then she tried a laser focus on the front five, looking for a badge, a sash, anything that marked them. Nothing. She stopped beside a woman handing out Kara Parshad from a huge steel bowl.

"Are the people at the front the Khalsa?" Brooke asked.

The woman laughed. "The Khalsa is all of us. Those five are just leading the singing."

Brooke looked back down the line, hundreds of marchers stretching toward the road, drums starting up somewhere near the front. She tried to summarize her findings to herself and got stuck, because the thing she had been looking for could not be counted or pointed at. It began in 1699, and it was here anyway, in the whole crowd.

Arjun ran up and grabbed her hand. "Come on, we're supposed to walk with everyone."

Brooke set down her cup and followed him into the street, where the drummers hit a rhythm and the crowd surged forward, buoyant, toward the sound.

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: Museums control temperature and humidity because changes make wood, paper and canvas swell and shrink, which can crack or warp old objects.
story:
Christopher counted the minutes until the bus left: forty, and he still hadn't found his grandfather's favorite painting. His grandfather had grown up in this city and had described a carved wooden door in the heritage wing so many times that Christopher could almost see it.

"Ten minutes in this room, then we meet at the exit," said the guide.

In the corner of the room, Priya stopped in front of a display case and tapped the glass. "There's a little gauge in there. Why does the painting need a thermometer?"

"That's for humidity," the guide said. "Museums control temperature and humidity because changes make wood, paper and canvas swell and shrink, which can crack or warp old objects."

Christopher filed that away and kept walking. Then he stopped. His grandfather had described the wooden door with a split running down one panel, and he had blamed the moving men. But the door had hung in this same museum for sixty years, and museums kept the air steady. If the crack had happened here, someone would have noticed and fixed it, wouldn't they? He had to check.

He found the door in the next gallery, tall and dark, behind its own glass. The split was there, thin as a pencil line, low on the left panel. A small card beside it read, "Cracked before acquisition, 1961." So the damage had happened before the museum got it. His grandfather's story about the moving men could still be true. Christopher revised his whole picture of the afternoon: the crack was old news, and the museum was protecting the door from new ones.

He took out his phone. "Priya, come here. You wanted a photo for your project, right?" She jogged over and framed the door, careful to catch the crack and the card together.

"Hold still," Priya said, and pressed the button twice.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: The Internet Archive's Wayback Machine has saved more than one trillion web pages, so something deleted from a public website can sometimes still be found.
story:
The bus smelled like wet jackets, and Mathis had his phone out under his backpack so the driver wouldn't see it. Dani slid into the seat beside him and leaned over.

"Did you check the club page this morning?" she asked.

"No," Mathis said. "Why?"

"Because your thing is still on it."

"My thing is gone. I deleted it last night." He opened the page anyway. There was the announcement he had written two weeks ago, the one that said the robotics club meeting was cancelled because, as he had put it, "our leader Mr. Ortega is afraid of the vending machine." Mr. Ortega had seen it. His mother had gotten an email. Mathis had deleted the post the second he got home.

"Scroll up," Dani said. "Priya screenshotted it, and now it's in the group chat."

He scrolled. Priya had posted the screenshot with three crying-laughing faces, and eleven people had replied. He typed a message into the chat, deleted it, typed another, deleted that too. In public posts you wrote one way, he had noticed, and in private chats you wrote another, all lowercase and jokes, and he had mixed the two up by accident. That was the problem. The post had sounded like a text to Priya, but anyone in the whole network of the school could read it.

"How old is the page?" Priya called from three rows back. She was leaning into the aisle, which was against the bus rules, but the driver was watching the road.

"Two weeks," Mathis said.

"Then it might be in the Wayback Machine."

"The what?"

She held up her phone so he could see the screen. There was a familiar page, but not the current one. It was the club page as it had looked days ago, with his post sitting there in the middle like it had never been deleted.

"That can't be real," Mathis said. "I took it down."

"It's real. It's called the Wayback Machine. It's saved more than one trillion web pages." Priya sat back down as the driver glanced in the mirror. "If a page was public, an old copy can sometimes still be found."

Mathis looked at his own phone. The bus rattled over the railroad tracks, and his grip on the phone felt frail, like the thing might slip out of his hands and take the last of his dignity with it. He opened the site Priya had shown him and typed in the club page's address. A calendar appeared. He tapped a date from two weeks ago. His post loaded, word for word, vending machine and all.

"So deleting it didn't delete it," he said.

"Deleting deletes it now," Dani said. "Not before."

He copied the link and pasted it into his message to Mr. Ortega, the one he had been drafting all morning. He wrote that he was sorry, that he had found where the old copy lived, and that he wanted to know if there was any way to retrieve it, or at least to explain it before anyone else did. Then he set the phone face down on his knee and watched the school come into view through the rainy window.

"Are you going to send that?" Dani asked.

Mathis picked the phone back up and pressed send.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: A pill organizer has a compartment for each day of the week, so an empty compartment shows that day's dose has already been taken.
story:
Alice pressed her nose to the glass at Gate B14 and watched the planes slide past like giant white birds. Grandma Ruth was somewhere behind that door, arriving for a whole week, and Alice had been rehearsing her welcome all morning. When the passengers finally streamed out, Grandma appeared pushing a small suitcase, her coat unzipped, her face tired but searching the crowd until it found Alice.

"There's my navigator," Grandma said, and hugged her hard enough to squeeze the air out of her.

At home, the week unfolded in small, ordinary ways. Alice showed Grandma the garden, where the bean seeds she'd planted in April had begun to germinate, pale green shoots pushing up through the soil. Grandma inspected them like a scientist and declared the whole row promising. But on Thursday morning Alice found her sitting at the kitchen table, staring at a plastic box with her pills, tapping her finger against the lid.

"I can't remember whether I took my morning pills," Grandma said. "It was such a scramble, your dad honking about the parking, and now I simply cannot recall."

Alice's first thought was that they should just call the doctor, but she knew Grandma would never agree to that, not over a small thing. Her second thought was sillier: maybe the pills could tell them somehow. Then she looked at the box in Grandma's hands. It wasn't one big jumble of pills. It was divided into separate little compartments, each one labeled with a day of the week, Sunday through Saturday. Thursday's compartment was empty. The others still held their pills, sitting there like tiny waiting passengers.

"Grandma," Alice said slowly, "if a compartment for each day is empty, doesn't that show the dose for that day was already taken?"

Grandma blinked, then held the box up to the window light. "Thursday's empty," she said. "I did take them. Your old grandma managed it after all." She laughed, and the worry slid off her face like a coat being unzipped. That afternoon they planted a row of marigolds together, and Grandma told a story about a bird she'd once nursed through a virus, a pale thing she'd found during a migratory season when the sky above her old farmhouse seemed made of wings.

On Sunday, Alice drove with her parents back to the airport. At the security line, Grandma turned and pressed something into Alice's hand: a small spare pill organizer, brand new, days of the week printed along the top. "For when you're old and forgetful like me," she said. Alice slipped it into her backpack, next to a paper bag of the marigold seeds, and waved until Grandma's gray head disappeared down the corridor.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The first Super Bowl was played on January 15, 1967, and the Green Bay Packers beat the Kansas City Chiefs 35 to 10.
story:
Grandpa Ray kept saying he remembered the very first Super Bowl like it was yesterday. "Best day of January, 1967," he announced from his recliner. "January fifteenth, and the Packers destroyed the Chiefs, thirty-five to ten."

Luke looked up from his plate of nachos. Grandpa told great stories, but some of them changed depending on the day. Last summer he had claimed he once shook hands with a president, and when Luke asked which one, Grandpa had said, "The tall one." That answer had planted a small seed of doubt, and a little resentment too, because Luke wanted to believe him.

"You were there?" asked Marcus, Luke's cousin, from the couch.

"In my living room, glued to the TV," Grandpa said. "Cold as anything outside. Green Bay won it going away."

Luke decided to test this. Not by asking Grandpa more questions, because Grandpa could simulate confidence about almost anything. Instead, Luke slipped into the hallway, found Grandpa's old photo album on the shelf, and flipped through the pages until he reached the late sixties. There it was: a black-and-white photograph of a television set, and on the screen, blurred but readable, two teams in motion. Tucked behind the photo was a yellowed scrap of newspaper. The headline said Green Bay Packers 35, Kansas City Chiefs 10, and the date printed above it was January 15, 1967.

Luke carried the album back into the den and held it open in front of everyone. "Checked your math, Grandpa."

Grandpa put on his reading glasses, looked for a long moment, and grinned. "Told you. Thirty-five to ten."

"Okay," Luke said. "You get to keep the story."

Marcus groaned as the teams lined up for the second half. "Why are you two so calm? We're losing by two touchdowns."

"That's pessimistic," Grandpa said. "The Packers were down once, way back when. And look how that turned out." He pointed at the album still lying open on Luke's knees.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: A swimmer caught in a rip current can usually escape by swimming parallel to the beach, out of the narrow current, rather than straight against it.
story:
Aunt Carol's house sat two blocks from the ocean, and on the first morning of the visit Emma's cousin Theo ran straight for the beach with a boogie board under his arm. Emma followed, but she stopped at the wooden sign near the lifeguard tower. It showed an arrow pointing sideways along the waves and a warning about rip currents.

"What's a rip current?" Theo asked, squinting up at it.

The lifeguard, packing up her umbrella, called over, "It's a narrow strip of water that pulls you out away from the beach. If you get caught, swim parallel to the beach, out of the current. Don't fight it straight on."

Emma studied the water. Theo was already splashing, but she wanted to see if she could spot the danger before anyone had to escape it. She noticed a gap in the line of breaking waves, a lane of smooth, darker water pushing outward, narrow like a corridor between two churning stretches of white. That must be it. She could almost categorize the whole surf into two kinds: rough and breaking on both sides, smooth and pulling in the middle.

She kept watching while Theo's older sister Marisol helped her set out towels, careful with the old paperback Marisol was reading, its spine cracked and its brittle pages yellow from salt air. Emma rotated the umbrella so the shade would reach Marisol's chair, then sat down to keep watch.

Later, when Theo let the board drift and the smooth lane caught him, Emma was already running. She had told Marisol where the gap was, and Marisol was waving the lifeguard down, but Emma reached the surf first and swam hard, angling sideways, parallel to the beach, stroking and stroking until the pull let go of her. She grabbed Theo's arm and they rode a breaking wave in together.

They collapsed on the sand, coughing and laughing. Theo hugged the boogie board like a pillow. "You went sideways," he said. "Just like the sign."

"That was the whole point," Emma said, and shook the water out of her hair.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A note's pitch depends on how fast the sound source vibrates: faster vibration makes a higher pitch, and slower vibration makes a lower one.
story:
The garage smelled like motor oil and old tennis shoes, and Ruby sat on an upturned milk crate with her aunt's secondhand guitar across her knees. She had wanted this guitar all summer, ever since she traded away her keyboard at the neighborhood swap and instantly regretted it. Now she had it, and the thickest string made a warbly, low sound that didn't match the tutorial video at all.

She turned the tuning peg a little and plucked the string. The note slid down, lower and lower, like a balloon losing air. She turned it the other way and plucked again, and the note climbed back up. She tried it once more just to be sure. Something invisible was changing here, and she wanted to pin it down. Her little brother Theo, who was supposed to be sweeping but was instead flicking a rubber band at the wall, wandered over.

"Listen," Ruby said. She plucked the tight string, then loosened the peg and plucked again. "Hear how it goes low when the string is floppy?"

"It's just a string," Theo said, and flicked his rubber band. It made a dull thud. He stretched it tighter between his fingers and plucked it, and it gave a squeaky, high twang that seemed to propel itself across the garage.

"Exactly like mine," Ruby said, staring at the rubber band. "Loose and slow means low. Tight means the string is moving faster, so the pitch goes up." She said the word pitch carefully, trying it out, because the video had used it and now it finally made sense. It wasn't about how hard you plucked; she tested that next, plucking gently and then hard on the same tight string. The volume changed but the note stayed put. It was the speed of the wiggling that mattered, and she couldn't see the wiggling at all, only hear it.

Theo dug through a drawer and came back with a thick polymer bracelet, one of those stretchy bands, and a skinny green one from a party favor. The thick one, plucked, rumbled low. The skinny one, pulled taut, whined high. "This one's basically toxic green," Theo said, holding it up, and Ruby laughed and took it from him.

She tuned the big string by ear, listening, adjusting, listening again, until it rumbled like the video's. Somewhere in the middle of all that careful listening, she thought about the keyboard she'd traded away, how she'd given it up because it seemed too easy, and she wondered whether easy things were worth less or whether she'd just been impatient. She didn't decide. She just played the string once more, and it held its note, steady and low.

"Again," Theo said, holding out the green band. "Do the tight one."

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Blue-enriched light from phone screens can reduce or delay the body's release of melatonin, the hormone that makes you sleepy in the evening.
story:
Owen's new phone arrived on a Saturday morning, and he carried it around the house like it was made of glass. He set his wallpaper to a picture of a comet, added his best friend Marcus's number, and learned to type with his thumbs faster than anyone in his family believed possible. That first night, he scrolled in bed until eleven, looking at videos of skateboard tricks and a mild controversy about which cereal was best. Then he lay in the dark, wide awake, staring at the ceiling.

The same thing happened Sunday night, and Monday night too. Owen was not worried about anything, and he had not drunk any soda, so those explanations were out. On Tuesday he made a list on a napkin: awake at eleven, awake at midnight, awake at twelve thirty. The only thing different about those nights was the phone. "A pattern," he said to himself. "Screens in bed, then no sleep." He had a theory, and he knew exactly how to test it.

On Wednesday he left the phone on the kitchen counter at bedtime, told Marcus he'd text him in the morning, and got under the covers. He fell asleep so fast he barely remembered closing his eyes. Thursday he took the phone to bed again, and again he tossed for over an hour. Friday, no phone, and he was asleep before his dad came upstairs to check on him. Two Fridays' worth of proof was better than one.

Saturday morning he found his older sister Maya in the kitchen and told her the whole experiment. "So the light delays the melatonin," she said, nodding. "That's the hormone that makes you sleepy in the evening." She said their cousin had the same problem last year. Owen felt like a scientist with a legitimate discovery, even if a million people already knew it.

He typed a new rule into his phone's notes app, in all capitals: PHONE SLEEPS IN THE KITCHEN. Then, because one rule deserved a backup plan, he set an alarm labeled BEDTIME and dragged the phone icon across the counter, far from the stairs. "You can intervene in my sleep all you want," he told it, "but only until nine o'clock." The phone sat there glowing, and Owen ran upstairs two steps at a time to beat the alarm.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: On the Holmes and Rahe stress scale, published in 1967, both changing residence and changing schools are listed as life events that require readjustment.
story:
The cafeteria smelled like disinfectable and overcooked noodles, and Kaitlyn counted the tables without meaning to. Fourteen tables, and at every one, the kids had already sorted themselves into groups that closed like fists. Her stomach, which had never had a brave constitution, twisted as she carried her tray toward the empty table by the window. In Maplewood she would have walked straight to Priya's table and stolen a fry without asking. She wondered now whether she should have hugged Priya longer on the last day, instead of waving from the car like someone in a hurry to leave.

The school counselor, Ms. Anaya, had pulled her in that morning for a five-minute welcome chat. Kaitlyn mostly remembered the bowl of wrapped candies and the pamphlets fanned across the desk. While Ms. Anaya answered the phone, Kaitlyn had slid one pamphlet closer. Its title was Stress and Life Events, and inside was a checklist from something called the Holmes and Rahe stress scale, published in 1967. It listed life events that required readjustment, and there, two lines apart, sat "change in residence" and "change in schools." Both. On the same list, as if two ordinary things could gang up on a person.

She had tested the idea all day like a science experiment. Prediction: if the list was right, other kids who had just moved should feel the same wrecked way she did. So in third period she scanned the room for anyone looking lost, and in the hallway she watched for kids eating lunch alone. She spotted exactly one, a boy in a green hoodie drawing in a sketchbook at the table next to the trash cans.

"Is that a fox?" she asked, setting her tray down across from him.

"A lynx." He tilted the page toward her. "I'm Desmond. I moved here three weeks ago from Tucson."

Kaitlyn leaned in, suddenly unable to keep it to herself. "I found this thing in the counselor's office," she said. "It's called the Holmes and Rahe stress scale. Published in 1967. It's a list of life events that need readjustment, and changing where you live and changing schools are both on it." She hesitated, then chose not to disclose that she'd basically stolen the pamphlet, which was still folded in her back pocket like contraband. "I've been testing it. You look about as terrible as I feel."

Desmond laughed, a short surprised bark. "Three weeks in and I still get lost going to gym. Yesterday I walked into the boys' bathroom on the wrong floor."

"That's not stress," Kaitlyn said. "That's just a badly designed school."

He ripped a strip off his brown paper bag and wrote something on it, then slid it across the table. In blocky capitals it said NEW KID CLUB, MEETING PLACE: THIS TABLE, and underneath he drew two lynxes, one of them wearing her exact blue headband. Kaitlyn stuck it inside her notebook, next to the folded pamphlet, and stole one of his tater tots without asking.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: Ted Williams batted .406 in 1941 and is the last Major League Baseball player to finish a season above .400.
story:
Andrew pulled his stick back, aimed at the far corner, and watched the puck slap off the goalie's pad and skitter wide. That made him one goal on nine shots in the two practices the coach had charted. One for nine. He stood at the blue line, breathing hard, staring at the clipboard where the assistant coach kept the numbers.

"There's your shooting percentage," Coach Renner said, tapping the sheet, which lay flat and transparent inside its plastic sleeve. "Eleven percent. Numbers don't tell you everything, but they don't lie either."

Andrew skated over to the boards where his grandfather sat in the third row, mittens on his knees. Grandpa came to every Sunday practice even though he had never laced on skates in his life. He was a baseball man, and he loved numbers even more than Coach Renner did.

"Eleven percent," Andrew told him. "That's terrible, right?"

"Terrible or not, it's one number standing in for nine shots," Grandpa said. "One number, many events. Baseball does the same thing. Batting average. Hits divided by at-bats. I'll make you a bet, since you like numbers so much. I bet nobody in major league baseball has finished a whole season hitting .400 or better since before I was born, and I was born in 1948."

Andrew frowned. He knew .400 meant getting a hit four times out of every ten, which sounded almost easy until you thought about how fast a pitched ball travels. Still, in all those decades, with all those players, surely somebody had done it. He was twelve and he could already name a dozen sluggers.

"Bet," Andrew said. "If I win, you buy my hot chocolate for the rest of the season."

"And if I win, you carry my bag to the car every Sunday until the ice melts."

They shook on it through the gap in the glass. Grandpa's mittens were thick, and his handshake was gentle. Andrew skated back to the face-off circle, took ten more shots in the drill, and buried two of them, one high over the goalie's shoulder and one five-hole. Thirteen percent now, he figured, doing the division in his head while the Zamboni sat idling behind the far net like a patient yellow animal. Some players thrived under that kind of scoreboard pressure, and he decided on the spot that he was going to be one of them, whether the clipboard agreed or not.

After practice, in the lobby that smelled of popcorn and wet wool, Andrew sat on the bench with his grandfather's phone and looked it up. He scrolled past articles about Ted Williams, who batted .406 in 1941, and read it twice. Nineteen forty-one. The last player ever to finish a season above .400. Before 1948, before Grandpa was born. Andrew set the phone down slowly, the way you set down something you have lost to.

"Hot chocolate?" Grandpa asked, standing up and handing him his own bag to carry.

"One for nine," Andrew said, "is eleven percent. Two for twelve is sixteen. It goes up fast at the start."

"Everything does," said Grandpa, "until you're chasing .400."

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: When a phone takes a photo with location services on, it can write the exact GPS coordinates of where the photo was taken into hidden data in the file, called EXIF metadata.
story:
Alicia wanted to find out who kept sharing the photo of her falling into the pond at the class trip. It had been taken on Marcus's phone, and by Monday it was on three different group chats, passed along by people she didn't even know. She signed into a computer in the school lab during lunch, next to her friend Priya, and opened the original file Marcus had sent her.

"Look at this," Priya said, leaning over. She had right-clicked the photo and chosen "get info." A panel opened next to the picture, and inside it was a tiny map with a red pin. When Alicia clicked the pin, the map zoomed in and showed a street name she recognized, because it was her own street, right down to the end where the pond was.

"That's my house," Alicia said. "Why is there a map on a photo?"

Marcus was two computers over, so she went and stood behind him. "When you took that picture, was location on?"

He shrugged. "Probably. It's on for everything." He pulled up the same info panel on his copy, and the pin was there too, marking the exact spot. "It's in the file somewhere," he said. "Mr. Reyes called it EXIF metadata once. Hidden data in the picture file."

"So every photo knows where it was taken," Alicia said slowly, "and it travels with the photo." She thought about the three group chats, and the strangers who had forwarded the picture, and how each of them could open this same panel. It was like the photo was carrying her address in its pocket to everyone who received it.

At the next computer club meeting, Alicia asked if they could make the photo-sharing rules part of the club agreement, and the group spent twenty minutes negotiating over what counted as asking first. Marcus suggested that turning off location before taking pictures should be voluntary, not a rule, since it was each person's own phone, and Priya argued that anything with a map pin in it should never go to a group chat at all. By the end of the negotiation they had a written agreement, and fourteen signatures.

Alicia tested her idea that same afternoon. She took a photo of the whiteboard with location on, sent it to Priya, and asked her to check the info panel. Priya found the pin on the lab's street. Then Alicia turned location off, took the same photo, and sent it again. Priya opened the panel and looked for a long moment before turning the screen around. "Nothing," she said. "No map. Just the picture."

activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
knowledge_domain: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
fact: Chiaroscuro, an Italian word meaning 'light-dark', is the name for using strong contrast between light and shadow to make shapes look solid.
story:
Alexander sat on the floor of the gallery's Renaissance room with his sketchbook open and a lumpy gray sphere drawn on the page. His art homework was due tomorrow morning, and Mrs. Ruiz had circled his attempt three times already with red pen. "Where is your light coming from?" she had written. He could draw a circle, but every time he tried to shade it, the thing looked flat, like a sticker of a ball instead of a ball.

He had come to the gallery because his mother worked Saturdays at the front desk, and because the gallery was free, and because he was out of ideas. He got up and walked along the wall of old paintings, past a portrait of a man holding a letter. The label beside it read, "The artist's use of chiaroscuro gives the face its dramatic depth." He stopped. There was that word again; it had been on the vocabulary list Mrs. Ruiz handed out Monday, and he had ignored it. He copied it into his sketchbook, then looked hard at the painting. The man's forehead was almost white. One cheek slid into darkness so deep it merged with the background. Somewhere beneath the chin, a pool of black spread across the man's collar.

Alexander's older sister Dani found him there twenty minutes later, when her shift at the café ended. "Mom says we leave in fifteen minutes," she said, tapping her watch. "You're staring at that guy like he owes you money."

"Dani, what does chiaroscuro mean?"

She shrugged. "Italian. Light-dark. It's the name for using strong contrast between light and shadow to make shapes look solid." She said it fast, the way she recited stuff for her own classes, and drifted toward the bench.

Alexander sat down on the bench and turned back to his sketchbook, but he didn't draw yet. He was thinking about something he couldn't see: where the light was. In the painting, the man's nose threw a shadow to the left, which meant the light came from the right, from somewhere outside the frame, a window the painter never showed. The dark pool on the collar wasn't part of the man at all; it was a cast shadow, the head blocking the light from reaching the cloth. That was the rule. The ball in his drawing needed the same thing: a hidden light source, somewhere off the page.

He borrowed Dani's phone, set his eraser on the bench, and turned on the flashlight, holding it steady to the right and slightly above. The eraser's side grew pale at one bright point, curved into gray, and dropped into black, and a long soft shadow stretched leftward across the wood. He had ten minutes before closing. Working fast, he kept his pencil strokes tight, an economy of lines rather than scribbled layers, and made the highlight a small untouched patch of white paper, as assertive as the painted man's forehead. Where the sphere met the table, he pressed down hard and let the shadow spread behind it. When Dani called his name from the doorway, he looked at the page. The sphere sat there, round and heavy, like something you could pick up. He closed the sketchbook gently, so as not to smudge it, and ran for the door.

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: The Gunnery camp, begun in 1861 by Connecticut schoolmaster Frederick W. Gunn, who led his students on a hike to a camp by the sea, is usually considered the first organized American summer camp.
story:
Grayson had exactly one plan for surviving his first night at Camp Wabanaki: sit near the fire, say nothing, and count the days until pickup. Then the kid next to him, a loud boy named Teo, leaned over and said, "You're Grayson, right? You're in my cabin. Do you snore? Because a rodent got in our cabin last year and chewed a hole in my pillow, and I don't need two problems."

"I don't snore," Grayson said, which was true, though he had no idea what he'd do about a rodent.

The whole camp had gathered for the mandatory opening campfire, and the director, a woman everyone called Kat, pointed at a wooden plaque nailed to a big pine behind the fire ring. "Before we sing, look at that," she said. "Take it in. You're part of something old."

Grayson squinted through the smoke, which drifted up in slow ropes while the damp above the flames began to condense into a white cloud. He could only read a few words from where he sat: GUNNERY, 1861. He nudged Teo. "What's the Gunnery?"

"No clue. Race you to the plaque."

They scooted around the fire while the first song started, and there it was. The Gunnery camp, begun in 1861 by Connecticut schoolmaster Frederick W. Gunn, who led his students on a hike to a camp by the sea. It was usually considered the first organized American summer camp.

Grayson read it twice. Summer camp had always seemed like something invented for kids like him, recently, maybe by people with canoes and too many whistles. But no. It went all the way back to 1861, before his grandmother's grandmother. A schoolmaster had taken his students on a hike to a camp by the sea, and that had started everything, all the way down to this fire and his damp sneakers.

"Hey," Teo said. "I bet the lake is warm. Want to test it right now?"

Grayson stared at the plaque one more second, then grinned. "First one to the dock."

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: A cow's stomach has four compartments, and the first, the rumen, holds microbes that help break down tough grass the cow later brings back up and chews again as cud.
story:
The bus rattled past three barns before Leo found the note in his pocket again. It read "Audition, 2:00, band room, do not be late," and under it his mother had drawn a small trumpet. He folded it and put it away. Mr. Pruey stood at the front of the bus and held up a clipboard. "We board the bus back at noon sharp," he said. "The farm is forty minutes from the school, so if you are not on this bus, you are walking."

Leo sat beside Dana, who kept a running list of everything she saw out the window. "Cow," she said. "Another cow." Leo looked anyway, because the cows reminded him of his grandfather's farm two summers ago. He remembered standing at a fence while his grandfather pointed at a brown cow whose jaws moved side to side, slow and steady, even though there was no grass anywhere near its mouth. "She's working on something she already ate," his grandfather had said, and then a tractor drove past and Leo never found out what that meant.

At the farm, the class crowded around a rail fence. A black and white cow stood on the other side, chewing the same way, mouth empty, eyes calm. "It's not eating anything," Dana whispered, and wrote "ghost cow?" in her notebook. A girl named Priya said maybe it was thirsty. Leo thought about his grandfather's words, working on something she already ate, and started watching the fence line where the hay was.

A farm worker with a wheelbarrow stopped long enough for Leo to ask how a cow could chew with nothing in its mouth. "It's chewing cud," she said, and walked on. Leo raised his hand and asked Mr. Pruey whether he could feed the cow through the fence. Mr. Pruey checked the clipboard and said yes, one handful of hay each. Leo held his handful out first. The cow took it, swallowed some of it almost right away, hardly chewing at all, then went back to that slow side-to-side motion. It had swallowed now and chewed later, which meant the chewing part happened after the food was already inside.

"They bring it back up," Leo told Dana. "That's what cud is." Priya asked why any animal would do that, and Leo said he had read the poster inside the barn, the one near the sink. The poster said a cow's stomach had four compartments, and the first one was called the rumen, and the rumen held microbes that helped break down tough grass, and after that the cow brought the grass back up and chewed it again. Dana copied it all down, even the word rumen. At noon the bus horn sounded, and Leo was the first one up the steps, holding his trumpet case and reading the note one more time.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: In February 2015 a photo of a dress went viral because some people saw it as blue and black and others as white and gold; the real dress was blue and black.
story:
Victor's older sister Nadia slid her phone across the dinner table so fast it nearly landed in the mashed potatoes. "Tell him," she said. "The dress in this photo is white and gold. Dad says it's blue and black. He's obviously losing his mind."

Victor picked up the phone and looked. The dress was blue and black. Obviously. He said so, and Nadia's face turned the color of the tomato sauce. "You're on his side? You were on my side about the movie last week!"

"You were right about the movie," Victor said. "This is different. It's blue. Like Dad's tie blue."

Their mother leaned over Victor's shoulder, squinted, and announced that the dress was white with gold lace. Grandpa, without even putting down his fork, said gold trim, white body, no question. The table split clean in half: Victor and Dad on one side, Nadia, Mom, and Grandpa on the other.

Last summer, Victor remembered, the whole family had collaborated on Grandpa's surprise birthday picnic, and even when the cake collapsed they had laughed together. That was the family he wanted back. He couldn't stand the idea of them fighting over a photograph until Christmas. He decided to test something. If everyone looked at the exact same picture at the exact same angle, would the answers still split? He passed the phone around the table twice more, making everyone hold it at arm's length, then close up. Same results, both times. His side stayed blue and black. The other side stayed white and gold. It wasn't a trick of the angle, and nobody was lying, either, because Grandpa looked genuinely sorry for him when he insisted the dress was white.

After dinner Victor snuck the phone into the hallway and searched the photo online. He found it everywhere. In February 2015, the picture had gone viral because people all over the world saw it differently. Some saw blue and black. Others saw white and gold. And the real dress, the actual dress in a real store, was blue and black. Victor read the last part twice, then walked back into the kitchen holding the phone above his head like a trophy.

"Blue and black," he said. "The real one. It's official."

Nadia crossed her arms. "Then why do I see white?"

Victor thought about how certain she'd sounded, and how certain he still felt. He pulled out a chair beside her instead of dancing around the table.

"I don't know," he said. "Want to look at it together?"

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The crowd 'wave' became known worldwide at the 1986 FIFA World Cup in Mexico, so many English speakers outside North America call it the Mexican wave.
story:
Carson had been at Mr. Okafor's living room since noon, squashed between his dad and his cousin Rodrigo on a sagging couch. The big match filled the screen, and the room thundered every time the ball got close to the goal. Only twelve minutes remained on the clock, and the score was still tied.

"Watch this," Rodrigo said, leaning forward as the camera panned across the packed stadium. "Here comes the Mexican wave." Around the huge bowl of seats, thousands of fans stood up and threw their arms overhead, one section after another, like a ripple rolling all the way around and back. The whole living room jumped up and did it too, even Mr. Okafor, who nearly knocked over a lamp.

"The wave, you mean," Carson said.

"Not where I live. In Mexico we call it the Mexican wave. It became famous at the 1986 World Cup there, and people all over the world took the name from us."

Carson sat back down, thinking. He had always just called it the wave, the way everyone at school did. But Rodrigo wasn't joking; his face had that serious, slightly proud look. Carson wondered how the same thing could have two names on two sides of somewhere invisible, a border you couldn't see from a couch. Maybe the name traveled the way the wave itself did, section by section, country by country. There was only one way to find out.

"Mr. Okafor," Carson called over the noise, "when you were a kid in Nigeria, what did you call it?" Mr. Okafor scratched his chin. "The Mexican wave," he said. "Everyone I knew did." Then Mrs. Vidal, from the kitchen doorway, shouted that her whole family in Argentina said the same thing. Carson grinned. His test had worked. Only his dad shrugged and said, "Huh. We always just said the wave."

"You see?" Rodrigo said, pointing at Carson like he had scored a goal himself. "Two names, one move." Carson filed that away, next to a memory from last summer when he had told a new kid at camp that everybody called freeze tag the same thing, and the kid had laughed and said his neighborhood called it statues. He'd argued about it for a whole afternoon. Maybe he should have just asked around, like tonight.

On the screen, a striker broke free, and the crowd noise rose like a turbine winding up. Mr. Okafor leapt to adjust the antenna, calibrating it with tiny twists until the picture cleared, and everyone agreed it was a legitimate emergency because the ball was in the box. Then the whole room, all eleven people, rose in one motion and did the wave themselves, arms sweeping up toward the ceiling, and Carson stood last, on purpose, the way the final section always does.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: During Mexico's Dia de los Muertos on November 1 and 2, families build altars called ofrendas with photos and marigolds, whose color and scent are said to guide spirits home.
story:
Luke had never built anything for a dead person before, so he stood in Grandpa René's garage with a shoebox of Grandma Elena's photos and no idea where to start. It was November 1, and Grandpa had spent the morning being meticulous about a wooden table in the corner, wiping it three times and setting out sugar skulls in rows as straight as soldiers. Luke's little cousin Mateo circled the table like a shark, clearly wanting one particular skull with blue icing.

"On November first and second, we build ofrendas," Grandpa said, tapping the table. "Altars. Her photo goes here."

Luke chose the photo from the wedding, the one where Grandma laughed so hard her glasses slid down. He set it in the center. Grandpa handed him a basket of marigolds, whole ones and loose petals, and told him the color and the scent were said to guide spirits home. Luke studied the doorway, then the table, and laid a trail of petals across the floor from the front door to the photo. If the scent was supposed to lead her, then a path made sense. He tested it by walking it himself, nose down, and the sharp orange smell followed him the whole way.

"That's a good adaptation," Grandpa said. "She always did come in through the front door, even when the porch was flooded and everyone else used the back."

Mateo stopped circling long enough to announce that he had changed his mind about the blue skull, because the yellow one had more teeth painted on, and teeth meant it could fight. He put the blue one back and carried the yellow one around like a bodyguard. Mom, who had prescribed fresh air and errands as a cure for everyone's gloominess that morning, sat down instead and didn't leave.

Luke added one last petal directly under the photo, then a second one, because Grandma Elena had always said anything worth doing once was worth doing twice. From the doorway the trail glowed orange in the lamplight, a straight line from the world outside to her face on the table.

"She'll find us," Mateo said, holding up his sugar skull. "I brought backup."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: The word Inuit means 'the people' in the Inuktitut language, and one person is called an Inuk.
story:
Eli had come to Micah's house to finish their project poster, and so far they had finished two bowls of popcorn and a debate about whether microwaved cheese counted as nutritious. The poster itself still needed a caption for the photo of Micah's grandmother, who was on the wall of the community centre in a display about northern artists.

"Write this," Micah said, licking marker off his thumb. "Grandmother Olemaq, an Inuit, in 1962."

Eli printed it out in his best capitals, then stopped, pen hovering. "Wait. Is that right? An Inuit?"

"How would I know?"

"You're the one with the grandma in the photo."

Micah squinted at the poster the way his dad scrutinized the router whenever the internet died during a recession, which his dad claimed was every week lately. "She says Inuit all the time. Like, 'we are Inuit.' But she never says 'I am an Inuit.' She says..." He trailed off and marched toward the kitchen, where his grandmother was actually sitting, eating soup, which Eli took as a good sign.

She looked at the poster, then at Eli, then at her soup, in that order.

"Inuit means 'the people,'" she said. "One person is an Inuk."

"So it's 'an Inuk, in 1962,'" Eli said slowly, working it through. "One person, one word. Lots of people, the other word."

"You could put it that way," she said, and went back to her soup, which appeared to be more interesting than their poster.

Eli carried the poster back to the table, crossed out the wrong word, and rewrote it. Micah leaned over his shoulder, reading aloud in a news anchor voice. "Grandmother Olemaq, an Inuk, in 1962. Very dignified. She'd better see this before we glue anything."

"Better glue it fast, then," Eli said, and reached for the glue stick.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Complementary colors sit opposite each other on the color wheel, such as red and green, and mixing two complementary paints produces a dull brown or gray.
story:
Hunter had repainted his sunset four times, and every time the sky turned muddy. The craft shed smelled like pine and paint, and his wooden plaque sat in front of him with a sky the color of wet dirt.

Across the table, Marta leaned over her friendship bracelets and squinted at his project. "It was orange this morning," she said. "What happened?"

"I tried to make the part near the mountain darker, so I mixed in some blue," Hunter said. "Then I added orange again to fix it. Then more blue." He held up his brush like evidence. "Now it's brown."

Rafi, a veteran camper who had come to Lake Birch for six summers in a row, wandered past with a cup of juice. He looked at the plaque and winced. "That happened to my dragon one year. I never figured it out."

That was the problem, Hunter thought. He could see the mud, but not what was making it. It wasn't the brushes, because Marta had used the same jars and her flowers stayed bright. It wasn't the wood, because his practice stars on scrap wood had turned brown too, and they had been fine on paper.

He got a fresh scrap of wood and laid out four dabs: orange and blue, red and green, yellow and purple, blue and yellow. He mixed each pair with a clean craft stick. The blue and yellow cooperated beautifully, turning into a green that looked like the lake in July. The other three mixes all went dull and brownish, like somebody had spilled dirt in them.

"Look at this," he said, and Marta and Rafi crowded in.

"So some colors get along and some don't," Marta said.

Hunter found the paper color wheel taped inside the paint box lid, the one nobody ever used. He spun it around. Orange sat straight across from blue. Red sat straight across from green. Yellow sat straight across from purple. Every pair that had turned brown sat opposite each other.

"The ones across from each other make the mud," he said. He tapped the wheel. "I heard the word once. Complementary colors. They're opposites, like red and green, and mixing two complementary paints gives you a dull brown or gray."

"So your sunset turned brown because orange and blue are complementary," Marta said.

"Opposite each other," Rafi said, tracing the wheel with his finger. "I could have saved my dragon."

Hunter painted the dark part of his sky with a blue that leaned toward purple's side of the wheel, and only a whisper of it, keeping the orange far from the edge. The sky glowed. Down at the bottom, he painted the mountain gray on purpose, which felt almost like a joke.

"That's the best one in the shed," Marta said.

Hunter signed his name in the corner with the smallest brush.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: In his book Opticks, first published in 1704, Isaac Newton arranged the colors of the spectrum in a circle, an early form of the color wheel.
story:
Aaron had been at Camp Winnow for four days, and his craft project was already a disaster. He was supposed to make a spinning color wheel, a cardboard circle painted with wedge-shaped sections of color. When you spun it fast, the colors were supposed to blur together. His first attempt had gone wrong because he'd painted the wedges in a random order, and when the disc spun, it looked like mud.

The problem, he decided, was the order of the colors. Something about how they sat next to each other mattered, but he couldn't see it directly. He could only see the muddy result. So he tried an experiment. He painted a second wheel with red next to green, and blue next to orange, opposite pairs facing each other across the circle. Then he spun both wheels side by side and compared them. The second one blurred into something smoother, less brown. There was a rule hiding in there somewhere, and he was going to find it.

He went looking for information. The craft shed had exactly one bookshelf, holding a bird guide, a mystery novel missing its last thirty pages, and a dusty paperback called Opticks by Isaac Newton. Aaron flipped through it, mostly to be polite to the bookshelf, and stopped at a diagram. It was a circle, and the colors of the spectrum were arranged around the rim, red blending into orange, then yellow, then green, then blue. Newton had done this, the title page said, in a book first published in 1704. "Guys," Aaron said to the two boys painting beside him, "Newton drew one of these. Isaac Newton. In Opticks, 1704, he put the spectrum colors in a circle."

"Newton?" said Marcus, who was building a rubber-band-powered propeller out of a ruler and two plastic spoons. "The gravity guy? Why would he care about paint?" Marcus had spent the whole week insisting that crafts were a waste of time and real science was the only thing worth doing. Now he leaned over Aaron's shoulder and studied the circle for a long moment. "Huh. Okay, crafts, science, same shed," he said, and abandoned his propeller to grab a blank cardboard disc.

That night Aaron wrote a letter home, because the camp had a no-phones rule and his mother had promised to send real stamps. "Dear Mom," he wrote. "You were vague about what camp would be like, and you were right not to explain, because I would not have believed it. I made a color wheel. Mine failed at first, so I isolated the problem by testing one thing at a time, and it turns out a man from 1704 had already figured out the order. Tomorrow Marcus and I are painting his wheel with the spectrum going around in a circle, exactly like Newton's. Also, nobody has fed the camp hamster since Tuesday and I think that is the counselors' plan to make us think it is a mystery. Your son, Aaron."

The next afternoon they finished Marcus's wheel and spun it with the drill Marcus had borrowed from the maintenance shed. The colors blurred into a pale shimmer, and Marcus whooped so loudly that a counselor came running from the lake. "We got it," Marcus said, holding up the spinning wheel. "Newton's circle, spinning."

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: A 2006 study by Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke found that testing yourself on material helps you remember it longer than simply rereading it.
story:
The word list for the school spelling bee had forty words, and Hailey had read all forty of them eleven times by Tuesday night. Her little brother, Marco, kept drumming his pencils on the table, which began to irritate her so much that she finally slammed her list down. "Rereading isn't even working," she said. "I read the words and two seconds later I can't spell 'rendezvous.'"

Her dad looked up from his magazine. "Interesting. There's a thing in here about that."

He slid the magazine across the table. Hailey read the paragraph twice. "In 2006," she said slowly, "these researchers, Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke, found that testing yourself on material helps you remember it longer than simply rereading it." She frowned. "So instead of reading the list again, somebody should just quiz me."

"Want to try it?"

"Okay, but don't go in order," Hailey said. "If you go in order, I'll just remember which word comes next instead of the word itself. That would be a bias toward the list, not the spelling." That part seemed logical to her, and her dad agreed it was fair.

So every night he called out random words while she dried dishes or brushed her teeth. Marco turned it into a game, shouting words from the hallway like a game show host. On Thursday she missed "chrysanthemum" three times, and by Saturday she could spell it while hanging upside down off the couch.

Monday morning, Mrs. Tanaka's classroom smelled like whiteboard marker, and twenty-three chairs had been pushed back to make room for the finalists. Hailey's hands were cold even though the radiator was clanking. Devon, the boy who had won last year, stood beside her whispering the list to himself over and over, his lips moving like he was reading a secret letter.

"Rendezvous," said Mrs. Tanaka. "Devon."

Devon blinked. "R-e-n-d-e-z..." He stopped, stared at the ceiling, and started the whole list again in his head, searching for where the word had been on the page. "V-o-u-s?" It came out like a question.

The bell for the next round sounded, and Hailey touched his shoulder quickly. "Hey," she whispered, "want to come over tonight? My dad'll quiz us both." Devon nodded, and Mrs. Tanaka turned to Hailey with the card in her hand.

"Chrysanthemum," she said.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: When the price of one good rises, many buyers switch to a substitute, a similar good that does the same job, so demand for the substitute goes up.
story:
The price tag for Frosty Crunch cereal had jumped from four dollars to six, and Edouard stood in aisle five staring at it like it had insulted him personally. That cereal was the whole reason he had offered to come grocery shopping with his dad. He had plans for that cereal. He intended to consume an entire box by Sunday.

"Dad. Six dollars."

His dad picked up the box, checked the tag, and set it down beside its neighbor, Snow Puffs, which was still four dollars. "Interesting," he said, in the voice of a man who was not going to be interesting back.

Edouard looked at the shelf. The Frosty Crunch was nearly gone, one battered box left, while the Snow Puffs sat in a fat, untouched row. He narrowed his eyes with genuine skepticism. Frosty Crunch had been the popular one all year. Kids at school traded the prize toys at lunch. Maybe that was it. Everybody wanted it, there wasn't much left, and the store had raised the price. Meanwhile the shelf overflowed with Snow Puffs nobody loved, still cheap.

"So what do we do?" his dad asked. "You want the six-dollar box?"

Edouard picked up the Snow Puffs and studied the ingredients, the cartoon penguin, everything. It was basically the same food. Oats, sugar, a prize. "We buy this," he said. "It does the same job for four dollars."

"Since when do you eat Snow Puffs?"

"Since Frosty Crunch got expensive." He dropped it in the cart, feeling clever, and then he noticed something. Halfway down the aisle, the Kowalski twins were doing exactly the same thing, their mom pulling Snow Puffs off the shelf while one twin pointed sadly at the empty Frosty Crunch spot.

"Look at that," Edouard said. "Everybody's switching. The store's going to sell a million Snow Puffs."

"Congratulations," his dad said. "You've discovered the substitute."

Edouard frowned. "The what?"

At the checkout, the Kowalski twins were ahead of them in line. The older twin held up her box and said, "Frosty Crunch costs too much now, so we got the substitute. Same cereal, basically."

"Basically," Edouard agreed, and then, quietly, to his own box: "Better prize, though."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A batting average is hits divided by official at-bats, and walks do not count as at-bats, so the number gives a batter no credit for walks.
story:
The gym smelled like popcorn and floor wax, and the bleachers rattled every time the home crowd stomped. Lillian kept one eye on her sister's team and the other on her little brother, Dario, who was not watching basketball at all. He was hunched over a baseball card, scowling at it like it had insulted him personally.

"Reyes is the best player nobody talks about," Dario said, louder than he meant to. A man in front of them turned around, and Dario shrank, clearly intimidated. Lillian had compassion for him, mostly. She also wanted to watch the game.

"Then why does nobody talk about him?" she asked.

"Because his batting average is low. But it's wrong. It's not fair." He shoved the card at her. On the back, in tiny print, were numbers, and one row said AVG .243.

Lillian was systematic about things like this. She read the whole back of the card, row by row, while the crowd roared at a steal she missed. Hits. At-bats. Walks. She counted on her fingers, then counted again. "Wait. He has 60 walks and they're not in the at-bats."

"Walks don't count as at-bats," Dario said, shrugging. "That's just the rule."

"So the average is hits divided by at-bats." She tapped the card. "And walks aren't in there at all. He gets on base all those times and gets no credit for any of it. Not one."

Dario sat up straight. "Nobody at school believes me."

"Then write it down. Numbers in a note are harder to argue with than your face." She dug a pen out of her jacket. He grabbed a napkin from the popcorn bag and wrote, in huge letters, REYES GOT ON BASE 60 MORE TIMES THAN THE AVERAGE SHOWS. ASK ME HOW. He held it up so the man in front could see it.

The man read it, laughed, and turned back around. "Kid's got a point," he said to his friend.

The buzzer sounded, halftime, and the whole gym thumped with stomping feet. Dario folded the napkin carefully and tucked it into his pocket like a treasure map.

"Sixty," he whispered, grinning at the scoreboard for no reason at all.

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
fact: Shoveling heavy snow is hard work for the heart, so doctors advise taking breaks and lifting small loads rather than big shovelfuls.
story:
William woke to a strange brightness and a text from school: SNOW DAY, BUILDING CLOSED. He was already dressed before his mom finished her coffee. The snow had postponed his math test, which felt like a bonus prize, and the backyard lay under an ominous gray sky that promised even more by afternoon. Then he spotted Mr. Alvarez next door, standing at the top of his driveway with a shovel, breathing hard after only one narrow path. That gave William an idea, and maybe a job.

"Five dollars if I do the whole thing?" he called over the fence. Mr. Alvarez, who was sixty-eight and lived alone, agreed so fast it made William pause. He grabbed his shovel and marched over, ready to attack the driveway like the snow was the antagonist in one of his video games. He scooped huge, heavy shovelfuls, flinging them sideways, and finished one whole row before his arms burned. He noticed Mr. Alvarez had gone inside. Why would a man who wanted his driveway cleared go inside halfway through?

A girl came around the corner of the house, pulling a second shovel behind her like a sled. "I'm Rosa," she said. "He's my grandpa. I check on him on snow days." She looked at William's giant pile of thrown snow and then at the old man's footprints, which stopped and started, stopped and started, all the way up the first row. William followed her eyes. The pattern was there if you looked: Grandpa hadn't wandered off. He had been resting, over and over. "His doctor told him shoveling heavy snow is hard work on the heart," Rosa said. "He's supposed to take breaks." She pointed at William's shovel. "And lift small loads instead of big shovelfuls."

William looked down at his aching arms and wondered if his own heart was pounding the same way. He had been doing the exact opposite of everything, all at top speed. "So the trick is little scoops," he said slowly, "and we postpone the race part?" Rosa laughed and dragged her shovel to the far side. "You take that half, I'll take this one, and we rest between rows. Like circuits in gym."

They worked in small, easy lifts, and after each row they stood together at the edge of the driveway, watching their breath cloud in the cold. Mr. Alvarez came back out with a thermos and three cups of hot chocolate, and the work went faster with the breaks than William's solo sprint had, which seemed backwards until he thought about it. When they finished, the driveway was bare and William's arms felt fine. Mr. Alvarez pressed a five and a warm cup into his hands.

"Same time next storm?" William asked.

"Only if you promise to rest between rows," said Mr. Alvarez, and raised his cup like a toast.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: By convention, a graph puts the independent variable on the horizontal x-axis and the dependent variable on the vertical y-axis.
story:
Kaitlyn spread five sponge squares across the kitchen table, each one soaked in a different liquid: vinegar, salt water, lemon juice, cola, and plain water. Her question for the science fair was which liquid would erode a sponge fastest, and for two weeks she had weighed each square every night and written the numbers in her notebook. The sponges were polymers, her father had mentioned once, and apparently some liquids could wear that material down over time. Tonight she had to turn fourteen columns of numbers into one graph, because tomorrow morning the whole school would walk past her poster.

She drew her axes, taped on her labels, and stood back. Something felt wrong. Her bars climbed upward in a way that made cola look like it had no effect at all, when her notes clearly said the cola sponge had crumbled first. She flipped through her notebook, frowning, and flipped back.

The doorbell rang. It was Leo from down the street, holding his own poster under one arm. "Mrs. Talbot said you had the good markers," he said. "Can I borrow the red one? My volcano caption smeared." He came in, glanced at her graph, and then blinked at it. "Wait, why is time going up the side?"

Kaitlyn looked again. She had put the days along the vertical side and the sponge weight along the bottom, because the weight numbers had felt like the important part, the part that should stand tall. "Is that wrong?" she asked.

Leo set his poster on the counter. "My brother caught me doing that last week. The thing you change goes on the horizontal x-axis, and the thing that happens because of it goes on the vertical y-axis." He tapped her notebook. "You changed the days, and the weight happened because of that, right?"

Kaitlyn checked her notes. The days were what she had controlled. The weights were what had followed. "So the days go across the bottom," she said slowly, "and the weights go up the side." She pulled the tape off, rotated her labels, and redrew the bars. Now the cola line dropped steeply downward, and the plain water line barely bent at all, exactly the story her sponges had been telling her.

"That looks plausible now," Leo said, borrowing the red marker. "Want to come see whether my volcano still smokes?" She capped the marker and followed him out the door, poster under her arm.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: In science, a theory is not a guess; it is an explanation that has been repeatedly tested and supported, while a hypothesis is an idea still being tested.
story:
The puddle was back. Levi crouched beside the bathroom door in his socks and stared at the dark patch of tile, exactly where it had been yesterday morning. Nobody would confess. His sister Nadia wanted a new hamster cage and claimed a leaking pipe would finally wreck the floor enough that their parents would have to accommodate a whole renovation, which she said would be the perfect time for building shelves. Levi wanted the truth, and he had exactly one guess to test.

He spread flour in a thin white circle around the puddle, because whatever came through at night would leave tracks. He also set a cup under the sink pipe, in case the water came from there instead. His first idea, his best idea, was the cat. Before bed he told Nadia, "If the flour shows paw prints, I win."

At breakfast the flour told a different story. There were no paw prints at all. The cup under the pipe was bone dry, so that guess was dead too. But the flour itself had been disturbed, dragged in a long smear toward the bathtub, and there were marks in it that looked almost like small bare heels. Levi felt the hair on his arms rise. Nadia leaned over his shoulder and whispered, "Somebody walks in here at night."

They staked out the hallway at midnight. Levi's obligation was to stay awake, and he almost failed twice before the bathroom door creaked. Levi flicked on the light. Nadia stood at the sink, eyes open but somewhere far away, hands moving under the running tap. She had been sleepwalking. In the morning, embarrassed and fascinated, she flipped through the pamphlet from their last field trip and read aloud what the guide at the science centre had told her: "A theory is not a guess; it is an explanation that has been repeatedly tested and supported, while a hypothesis is an idea still being tested." Levi grinned. His sleepwalking idea had started as a hypothesis, and now, after the flour and the stakeout, it had support. Nadia shut the pamphlet and said, "Fine. But the shelves were still a fertile idea."

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: In a blind test, participants do not know which sample is which, so their expectations cannot sway their answers.
story:
Alexandre spread his science fair poster across the library table and frowned at the empty middle section. His experiment, a taste test pitting name-brand Crunch-O's against the store-brand cereal, had a problem. Yesterday his friend Marcus had sworn the name-brand box tasted better, and then admitted he had never even tried the store kind. How could Alexandre trust any answers if people already believed one box was the winner?

His little sister Priya wandered over from the lush tropical mural by the windows, where the painted vines looked greener than any real plant in town. She was eating dry cereal from a cup and clearly had opinions. Alexandre eyed her cup, then the two cereal boxes in his bag, and an idea began to form.

"Okay," he said, pulling out the boxes. "I need you to pour two bowls for me, but you have to hide the boxes first. Label them A and B and don't tell me which is which."

"Why?" Priya asked, already suspicious.

"It's a blind test," Alexandre said. "If I don't know which sample is which, what I expect can't sway my answers."

Priya hid behind the reference shelf with the boxes, and he heard her snickering the whole time. She returned with two matching bowls marked A and B in her careful handwriting. Alexandre tasted each one slowly, taking notes. Bowl A was slightly sweeter. Bowl B had a better crunch. He ranked them and slid his paper across the table.

Priya revealed the boxes, grinning. Bowl A, his top pick, was the store brand. He whooped so loudly that the librarian glared, and he shrank into his seat, still smiling. He could not accuse Marcus of lying about the name-brand after all; he had just proven that expectations do the talking when people know what they are eating. On his poster he wrote the comparison in fat letters: participants who could not identify the samples chose the cheaper cereal.

"Wait," Priya said, jabbing the nutrition labels. "The store one has fewer carbohydrates. Does that mean it's healthier?"

Alexandre looked at her, looked at his poster, and started a brand new page titled Round Two. "Get more bowls," he said.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: A 2016 world atlas of light pollution estimated that about 80 percent of North Americans cannot see the Milky Way from where they live, because of artificial light.
story:
The lights died at 8:17, right in the middle of Arthur's homework, and the whole house went quiet the way it does when the refrigerator stops humming. He found a flashlight and padded to the garage, where the breaker box waited with its rows of little black switches. He flipped the main one off and on. Nothing. He tried it again, slower, listening for the click. Still nothing, which meant the problem was not in his house at all. It was somewhere up the line, out on the street, invisible.

"Power's out for the whole block," his dad called from the porch. "Might as well come outside while it lasts."

The street was strange without its orange porch lamps and glowing windows. Arthur and his sister Maya stood on the grass, and Maya was the first to notice. "Look up," she said. "There are way more stars than usual." Arthur looked. The sky was crowded with them, a pale smudged river of light running across the dark. They argued about whether that river of stars was real or a cloud, and their dad mediated by suggesting they figure it out instead of shouting.

Maya still had battery on her phone. She searched and read out loud: "A 2016 world atlas of light pollution estimated that about 80 percent of North Americans can't see the Milky Way from where they live." She frowned. "It's called the Milky Way. That smudge."

"So that's it," Arthur said, working it through. "The streetlights and everything, all that artificial light, they wash it out. But tonight everything's dark." He thought of it like a simple equation: less ground light, more stars visible. He wanted proof. He clicked his flashlight on and held it near his face, staring upward. The faint stars closest to the horizon seemed to fade. He clicked it off, and they crept back.

"Try it again," Maya said, holding out her phone with its bright screen.

He did, twice more, and each time the stars near the light dimmed. Overhead a skein of migratory geese crossed the Milky Way, stitching a dark line through the pale river, and Arthur kept watching until the last of them passed.

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Title IX, a U.S. law signed in 1972, bans discrimination based on sex in schools that receive federal money, and it has been applied to their sports programs.
story:
Mason laced his cleats in the locker room, but his eyes kept drifting to the girl sitting two benches down, pulling on a helmet just like his. Her name was Priya, and she was trying out for the boys' baseball team with everybody else. A boy named Derek stomped over and said, "This is the boys' team. You can't be in here."

"The gym is open tryouts for baseball," Priya said calmly. "It says so on the sheet."

"There's a girls' softball team," Derek insisted. "So why would they let you..."

Mason wondered about that too. Why would the school run open tryouts if there was a whole separate team for girls?
