There had to be a reason, some rule working behind the scenes that nobody could see, like a current under the ice. He thought about how you might deduce it. If the school offered softball, that might be one factor, but maybe it wasn't the only one. Maybe the school had to let her try out no matter what.

"Come on," Mason said to Derek, "let's just go. Tryouts start in two minutes."

Out on the field, Coach Ramos set up a hitting rotation. Priya stepped into the cage fourth and smashed a line drive into the gap in left field. Derek stared. Mason noticed that Coach didn't even blink, as if a girl trying out were the most ordinary thing in the world. That was a clue. Coaches follow rules, Mason thought, even rules that aren't posted on the gym door.

After tryouts, he checked the athletic handbook on the bulletin board outside the locker room, running his finger down the pages. There it was, plain as a box score: Title IX, a U.S. law signed in 1972, bans discrimination based on sex in schools that receive federal money. And it had been applied to their sports programs. So that was the hidden rule. It covered the whole school, which meant Priya's tryout wasn't a favor or an accident. It was the law doing its quiet work.

The next day Mason found Derek by the lockers. "I figured out the Priya thing," he said. "It's Title IX, a U.S. law signed in 1972, banning discrimination based on sex in schools that receive federal money. It got applied to sports programs too. She has the same right to try out as us."

Derek frowned. "So my hypothetical girls-only baseball world isn't happening?"

"Not at this school," Mason said. He slung his bag over his shoulder. "Rosters get posted at three. Want to walk down and see who made it?"

Derek snapped his locker shut and followed him down the hall.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Feeling anxious sometimes is normal, but when anxiety is intense, lasts a long time and gets in the way of daily life, a doctor may diagnose an anxiety disorder, which is treatable.
story:
Alexa sat cross-legged on her bed with her science fair notebook open, but instead of taking notes she kept rereading the same paragraph about cloud formation. Every time she imagined standing up in front of the class tomorrow, her heart thumped like a drum and her stomach squeezed into a hard little knot. She pressed her palm against it and wondered what was actually happening in there. Could an intestine really tie itself up like a shoelace just because of a speech? That seemed absurd, and yet here she was, doubled over on her quilt over something her brother would call trivial.

She set the notebook down and called Priya on her tablet. Priya's face filled the screen, her bedroom closet visible behind her. "Okay, weird question," Alexa said. "Do you ever feel like your stomach is staging a protest before something big?"

Priya laughed. "I used to, every single morning before school. It wasn't just nerves, though. My mom noticed I wasn't sleeping and I kept fake-coughing to stay home, so we went to the doctor." She held up a hand before Alexa could ask. "The doctor said feeling anxious sometimes is normal. But mine was intense, it lasted months, and it was getting in the way of school and everything, so she diagnosed an anxiety disorder." Alexa repeated the words slowly, anxiety disorder, like she was testing whether they fit. "And here's the part that changed things," Priya went on. "It's treatable. I talked to someone and learned ways to cope, and now it's like... a smaller dog barking instead of a giant one."

Alexa wrote treatable in her notebook next to her cloud diagram. Then she had an idea, a small experiment. She grabbed the timer on her nightstand, set it for five minutes, and tried her new coping trick: breathe in for four counts, out for six, while naming three things she could see, hear, and touch. The lamp's warm glow. Rain ticking against the window. The ridges of her quilt under her fingers. When the timer buzzed, the knot in her stomach had loosened, not gone, but looser, like a fist uncurling one finger at a time.

"So it's like budgeting," Alexa said into the phone balanced on her pillow. "I budget my allowance for games and snacks. Maybe I can budget my worry, too, give it five timed minutes and then close the door on it." Priya snorted. "Boundaries for your brain. I like it." A knock rattled Alexa's bedroom door and her brother's voice came through: "Alexa, can I borrow your markers?" She took a breath and said, "Only if you knock and wait next time. That's my rule now." Priya cupped her hands around her mouth and called through the screen, "Boundaries for brothers, too!" Alexa laughed, picked up her marker, and drew a big circle around the word treatable.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: On drawing pencils, H is usually read as 'hardness' and B as 'blackness', so a 6B pencil makes darker, softer marks than a 4H.
story:
Scarlett raced through the library doors with her sketchbook under her arm and exactly forty minutes before the poster contest entries were due. The task was to draw your favorite place, and she had chosen the reading corner right here, with its worn green chair and the tall window behind it. She plopped down, grabbed a pencil from the shared box on the craft shelf, and started sketching fast.

The poster had to be bold. Judges walking past a wall of entries would give each one about two seconds. But when she held up her sketch of the chair, her lines looked pale and tired, as if the drawing itself wanted a nap. She scrutinized the paper, then the pencil, and noticed tiny letters stamped on the barrel: 4H. Last week, in Mrs. Okafor's art bin, she had grabbed a pencil stamped 6B and it had made rich, velvety darks. She turned the box over and found a jumble of Hs and Bs, all mixed together like camouflage, hiding the one she needed.

"I bet it's the letters," she whispered. She lined up four pencils on the table: 4H, H, 2B, 6B. One by one she drew a short stroke with each, pressing the same way each time. The 4H stroke was faint. The 6B stroke came out dark and soft as charcoal dust, darker than the 4H by a mile. She grinned so wide a boy at the next table looked over. "What are you doing, science?"

"Sort of," Scarlett said. "H is hardness and B is blackness. So this 6B is my new best friend."

She remembered the library's "shelf of eloquent posters," the fancy ones the librarians made for book month, and how their dark lettering had jumped out from down the hall. That was the look she wanted. With the 6B she redrew the chair, layered the window shadow until the paper seemed to glow, and added a cat curled on the cushion that had not been in her plan at all.

At the front desk she slid her entry across the counter with two minutes to spare. The librarian held it up to the light.

"Now that," the librarian said, "you can read from across the parking lot."

Scarlett said, "6B. Blackness."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A ranking shows order but not distance: first and second place might differ by a hundredth of a second or by a whole minute.
story:
Luca slid into the green plastic seat behind Dev and dropped his backpack like a gauntlet. Every kid on Bus 14 knew the rule: the last row belonged to whoever claimed it first, and all year Dev had conquered that row more than anyone else. His name sat at the top of the ranking Zuri kept on the fogged window with her finger, and Luca's name sat right below it, second, the way it had sat since October.

"Nine for Dev, eight for Luca," Zuri announced that morning, rewriting the tally marks. "Dev's winning sixty percent of the days so far. Luca's at fifty-three."

Dev grinned and stretched his legs across the whole row like a king. Luca stared at the tally marks instead of at Dev, because something about them had been bothering him for a week. The ranking said Dev was first and Luca was second, but the tallies said something the ranking didn't. He counted them twice, lips moving, while the bus jolted over the railroad tracks.

"Nine and eight," Luca said slowly. "You're only ahead by one day. One day out of thirty-some. But the ranking makes it look like you own the row." He tapped the fogged glass. "A ranking shows who's ahead. It doesn't show by how much. First and second could be a hundredth apart or a mile apart, and the list looks exactly the same."

"So?" Dev said, though his grin had gone a little brittle around the edges.

"So I'm not actually losing by much. I'm losing by exactly one day." Luca pulled out a notebook and wrote tomorrow's date at the top of a clean page. He had a plan: get to the stop ten minutes early, which was annoying, but one day would flip the ranking, and one day was all that separated them.

At the next stop, Marisol climbed on holding a crumpled paper. She'd been collecting signatures all week, and now she stood in the aisle and cleared her throat. "We took a ballot," she announced. "Vote on whether the back row gets rotated instead of raced for. It passed. Twenty-two to four."

Dev's mouth fell open. Ziri wiped the whole ranking off the window with her sleeve, tallies and all, and the fog closed over it like a curtain.

"Rotated," Dev repeated, staring at his sneakers.

Luca leaned back in the last row, which was suddenly nobody's row, and everybody's. "You know," he said, "I got here early today anyway."

"Yeah," Dev said. "By one minute."

"Thirty seconds," said Luca. "Check the tally."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A claim can be checkable even if nobody has checked it yet; 'most students at our school walk to school' could be tested with a survey.
story:
Gavin raised his hand so fast his chair scraped the floor. Mr. Okafor had just asked whether anyone could settle the argument Gavin and Priya had been having since Tuesday, and Gavin was not going to let the moment slip away. "Priya says most students at our school walk to school," he announced. "I think that's wrong. Almost everybody gets dropped off. The car line every morning goes all the way past the gym."

"That's your opinion," Priya said, arms folded. "You can't prove a thing by looking at one line of cars."

Mr. Okafor didn't jump in, which annoyed Gavin, because usually teachers jumped in constantly. Instead the class sat there with the question hanging in the air like the smell of disinfectant from the hallway. Gavin stared at the sparse corkboard by the window, where only two faded posters hung, and tried to think. He remembered last fall, when he'd claimed the cafeteria ran out of pizza by Wednesday, and Maya had counted for a whole week and shown it lasted until Thursday. He'd been wrong then, too, and it had stung, but not as much as being wrong without knowing would have.

"Wait," he said slowly. "It's not just an opinion. It's a claim. Like, it could be checked. Nobody has checked it yet, but we could." Priya tilted her head. "How?" she asked. "Follow everybody home?" Someone laughed. "A survey," Gavin said. "We ask every student how they get to school and count it up. Then we'd know if most of them walk or not." The word felt good in his mouth, solid, like a handle on a door he could actually open.

Mr. Okafor suggested they postpone the debate until they had data, and the class agreed to run the survey at lunch on Thursday. On Thursday, Gavin stood at the cafeteria door with a clipboard, pencil shaking slightly from too much excitement and not enough breakfast. The first twenty kids mostly said "bus," which surprised him. By the time the third lunch period started, his tally sheet was a mess of slashes and smudged graphite, but a pattern was climbing out of it anyway, one he hadn't predicted and Priya hadn't either.

They counted the sheets in Mr. Okafor's room after school, the radiator ticking, the hallway outside gone quiet. Priya totaled the walkers; Gavin totaled everyone else. He looked at her total, then at his own, then out the window at the empty car line loop, still painted yellow. "So I was wrong," he said, "but I was right that we could find out." Priya grinned and spun the clipboard toward him. "Count them again," she said. "I want to see your face when you get to the end."

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: Hormones in puberty make oil glands in the skin produce more oil, called sebum, which can clog pores and lead to acne.
story:
The zit had appeared on Sunday, right on the end of Emmett's nose, and school pictures were on Wednesday morning. He leaned against the car window while his mom drove, tilting the visor mirror to study it again, as if it might have shrunk since breakfast. It had not. His little sister used to get chocolate on her face and it wiped off with a napkin. This thing was different, and it seemed unfair that his own face would betray him two days before the photographer.

"Mom, can we stop somewhere? Like a pharmacy?"

She glanced over. "For what, honey?"

"Nothing. Face stuff." He felt his ears go hot. "Dad appointed me to pick up his razors anyway," he added, which was technically true, since Dad had said "grab me some razors if you're out" last week. Mom pulled into the parking lot of the drugstore by the hardware shop.

Emmett found the razor aisle first, then drifted to the wall of face washes, which was bigger than he expected. He was scanning shelves when a girl from his grade, Priya, appeared beside him, holding two bottles and turning them over to read the backs.

"Picture day?" she asked. "Me too. I woke up with three of them on my chin." She held up a bottle. "This one says it removes excess oil. My brother says pimples show up because of puberty. Hormones make the oil glands in your skin produce more oil, and it's called sebum, and it clogs your pores."

"Oil glands?" Emmett said. "I thought it was like dirt or something."

"That's what I thought. But it starts inside." She compared labels again. "So washing a million times wouldn't even fix it, because the stuff is coming from under the skin." She put one bottle back and kept the stronger one.

Emmett picked up a wash labeled for oily skin and read the back. The instructions were explicit: use twice daily, avoid eyes, rinse thoroughly. Twice daily. He counted backward. Two days until pictures meant four washes, if he started tonight. One wash right now in the store bathroom, one before bed, two more tomorrow and Tuesday. It wasn't much of a plan, but it was a plan, and having one made his shoulders loosen.

He paid with his own money, and in the car he read the bottle the whole way home, checking the ingredients like they were a code he might crack.

"Did you get your dad's razors?" Mom asked as they turned onto their street.

"Razors," Emmett said. "Right." He'd forgotten them completely. He ran back inside the store, grabbed the razors, and caught up with his mom at the register, the face wash in one hand and the razors in the other, four washes left before Wednesday.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: A fallen power line can still carry deadly electricity even when it is not sparking, so it should be treated as live, kept well away from, and reported.
story:
The lights went out at 7:40, right in the middle of Alexandra's homework, and the whole house sank into a black so complete she couldn't even find her own elbow. "The power's out," her little brother Marcus announced from the hallway, as if she might not have noticed.

Alexandra fished the flashlight from the kitchen drawer and did some thinking while Marcus bumped into the coffee table behind her. The streetlights outside were dark too, which meant it wasn't just their house. And on the walk home from school, after the storm, she had seen a wire lying across the sidewalk two blocks over. It had looked harmless, dull and quiet, not sparking or humming like wires in movies. But her science teacher had once said something Alexandra had never forgotten: a fallen power line can still carry deadly electricity even when it is not sparking, so it should be treated as live, kept well away from, and reported. Mr. Okafor had made them all repeat it twice, which had seemed ridiculous at the time and now seemed like the smartest thing anyone had ever done.

"Marcus, do not eat that cheese," she said, shining the flashlight on him. He froze with the block halfway to his mouth. "That's for dinner. It's the most nutritious thing we have until the fridge situation stabilizes." The situation, as far as she could tell, was that the temperature inside would fluctuate every time he opened the door to graze, and the cheese would not survive his snacking until morning.

Her phone was at nine percent, so she typed fast: "Mom. Power out on our street. I think it's the downed wire on Elm, two blocks from school. I saw it on the way home. I did NOT touch it, I stayed way back. Please call it in to the power company, my battery is almost dead." Send. The battery dropped to eight percent, then seven, as if to add commentary.

Twenty minutes later the porch lit up, the refrigerator hummed like a released prisoner, and headlights swept the window. Marcus cheered. Alexandra's phone buzzed once before it died: "Reported. Proud of you. Also I'm bringing pizza, keep your paws off the cheese." Alexandra laughed and hid the cheese behind the milk anyway.

activity: to solve two-step equations and plot the line they describe on a coordinate grid
knowledge_domain: to solve two-step equations and plot the line they describe on a coordinate grid
fact: In an ordered pair like (3, 5), the first number tells how far to move across along the x-axis and the second tells how far to move up or down.
story:
Michael stood at the counter of Delgado's Corner Store with four dollars and a math test folded in his back pocket, and he had a problem. The problem was that Mr. Pruitt had promised a pizza party for the whole class if anyone scored a hundred on Friday's test, and Michael was the only one even close. The other problem was the machine by the door.

It was an old claw machine, and today it held a single rubber ball with a coordinate grid printed on it, along with a few random prizes nobody wanted. Michael had already spent two dollars trying to grab that ball. The claw's grip seemed to evaporate every time it lifted, like his luck was steaming away into the air. If he could win the ball, he'd have the one study tool he actually wanted, because the ball showed equations and their lines, and lines were exactly the thing he couldn't picture.

"Four dollars," said Rosa, who worked the register and was in his sister Ana's grade. "You going to buy gum or feed that machine again?"

"Neither yet," Michael said. He unfolded the practice sheet Mr. Pruitt had given him. At the top, Ana had scrawled a battleship game from last night, where she'd sworn his shot at (3, 5) was a miss because he'd counted up three and over five instead of across first. They'd argued until their dad made them wash dishes.

Michael tapped the paper. If he solved for x, he'd get a number. Then he could put that number in the first slot of a pair and pick any number for the second slot, and plot the point. He tried it with 2x plus 1 equals 7. He subtracted the 1 from both sides in his head, then divided, and got x equals 3. So the pair started with 3, then across first, like Ana kept insisting. He drew a quick grid on the back of his receipt, marked (3, 5) by counting three across and five up, and marked (3, 0) too, and there they sat in a line going straight up and down, like a fence post.

"The first number is across," he said out loud. "The second one is up or down."

"So?" said Rosa.

"So the ball is the same thing." Through the scratched glass, every printed line on that rubber ball slanted upward at the same steady angle, and each label started with the x value. If he imagined the claw dropping at a spot three across from the left wall and five up from the bottom, he could aim it like a plotted point instead of guessing.

He fed in his last quarter, counted three across, five up, and pressed the button. The claw swung, dropped, and closed on the ball. It lifted. It held.

Rosa leaned over the counter. "Okay, that was not luck."

The claw carried the ball toward the chute, then stopped directly above it and opened its grip, one inch short of the drop. Michael stared. Then he grabbed the receipt, folded it into a tight wedge, reached through the prize flap, and nudged the ball the last inch until it tumbled into his hand.

"Friday," he told Rosa, holding it up. "Class pizza. Three across, five up."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: In traditional Chinese culture white is worn for mourning at funerals, while in many Western weddings the bride wears white.
story:
Grandma Wei arrived on Thursday, and by Friday night Isla had a problem: what to wear to her cousin Marisol's wedding shower on Saturday. Grandma had barely unpacked before she started pulling clothes out of Isla's closet and sorting them into two piles, one for yes and one for no.

"Not the white dress," Grandma said, holding up Isla's favorite one like it was a wet sock.

"It's a wedding thing," Isla said. "Marisol's whole theme is white. The invitations are white. The cake is white. The bride even wears white."

Grandma set the dress on the no pile and smoothed it flat, as if to preserve its feelings. "White is for mourning at funerals," she said. "In traditional Chinese culture, that is what we wear. For the dead." Then she pointed at Isla's rust-colored skirt. "Wear this."

Isla stared at her. She had never heard anything like this. Her brain started running its usual algorithm for arguments with Grandma: state facts, provide evidence, lose anyway.

Dad came through with the lasagna, and Isla got her chance. "Dad, tell Grandma white is a wedding color."

Dad put down the dish and rubbed his neck. "Both are true," he said. "Lots of Western brides wear white. And in Grandma's tradition, white is worn for mourning. Different people, same color, opposite meanings." He gave the no pile a guilty glance. "At your Aunt Po's funeral, everyone wore white. Marisol's wedding, the bride will too. Nobody's wrong."

Isla chewed on that through half a plate of lasagna. Same color. Two meanings. That meant the shower was going to be a room full of people doing opposite things at the same time, and only some of them would know it. She imagined Marisol's grandmother from Mexico, her neighbors, her own grandma, all handing gifts and thinking completely different thoughts about identical white napkins.

So she tested it. "Grandma, what if everyone at the party wears white except me? Won't I look like I'm at the wrong event?"

"Then you will look like the only person there with respect," Grandma said.

"That's a rebellious plan," Isla said. "Wearing not-white to a white party."

"Rebellious," Grandma agreed, spearing a meatball.

Isla tried one more angle. "Grandma, Marisol asked me to hand out the favors. White boxes with white ribbons. If I wear the rust skirt, the pictures will look strange."

Grandma put down her fork. For a moment Isla thought the algorithm had finally found a winning input. Then Grandma said, "The boxes are white?"

"Every single one."

Grandma looked at the window for a while. "Then the boxes are for mourning," she said, "and Marisol must pick new boxes, or I must pick new eyes." She picked up her fork again and went back to the lasagna. "Hand me the bread, and on Saturday you wear the rust."

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: U.S. sleep experts recommend 9 to 12 hours of sleep a night for children aged 6 to 12, and 8 to 10 hours for teenagers.
story:
Alexis laced his skates in the bench area of Riverside Ice Arena and watched his best friend Dante glide past the tryout line with his usual speed. That was the strange part. Dante was the fastest skater in sixth grade, but this morning he had wobbled twice during warm-ups, and when Coach Reyes blew the whistle, Dante's stop was so abrupt that he nearly fell over backward. Alexis filed that away and took his own turn around the cones.

The tryouts were for the school hockey team, and thirty kids had shown up to participate. Alexis wanted a forward spot, but so did Marcus Tran, who had been talking all week about how he was going to take it. Marcus was fast, too. During the second drill, Alexis noticed something. Marcus kept yawning on the bench. When the puck came to him, he reacted late, half a second behind, like a video with bad lag.

Between drills, Alexis sat next to him. "You look like you're skating through glue," Alexis said.

"I was up till two playing Starfall Six," Marcus admitted. "I only slept six hours. I figured I'd be fine."

Alexis had spent a week researching sleep for a science project, mostly so he could win arguments about bedtime. "Kids our age are supposed to get nine to twelve hours a night," he said. "Even teenagers only get to drop down to eight to ten. Six isn't on the chart for anybody."

"Whatever," Marcus said, and skated off, wobbling on the first turn.

Alexis thought about it while he waited for the scrimmage. He had a theory, one he couldn't see directly: the problem wasn't skating skill, it was an invisible cause, missing sleep, slowing everyone who had it. He could test it. His own plan had been to stay up nervous and wake at six, but instead he had gone to bed at nine thirty, and his legs felt springy on every crossover. When the scrimmage started, he cut left, took the pass, and scored on a rebound while Marcus watched the play arrive a beat too late.

At the end, Coach Reyes posted the list on the rink door. Alexis made forwards. Dante, who had crashed into the boards twice, made alternates. Marcus's name was not on the paper at all.

On the walk out, Dante pulled his hood up. "My cousin said there's a supplement for this. He's basically an entrepreneur, he sells protein powder to eighth graders out of his locker."

"Forget the powder," Alexis said. "Try nine hours."

Dante groaned. "That's so much sleeping."

Alexis pointed at the scoreboard clock, which still glowed above the empty ice. "You've got tryouts again in March. That's like ninety nights. You could test it properly."

Dante squinted at the clock, did some visible math, and said, "Fine. But if I turn into a grandpa who goes to bed at eight thirty, you're carrying my bag."

Alexis swung his own bag over his shoulder and said, "Deal," and the doors hissed shut behind them.
